source.title: Holiday Attire for Men: What It Means & How to Wear It
source.author: Gentleman's Gazette

tips.text: When a holiday party's dress code is unclear, lean towards the formal end, unless the hosts have said it's a playful ugly-sweater party.
tips.why: Nobody faults a guest for looking put together.

tips.text: If you're unsure what a holiday invitation expects, ask the hosts directly.
tips.why: Following their dress code is a courtesy.

tips.text: Read 'holiday attire' as cocktail attire with a festive touch, such as tartan or a seasonal colour.
tips.why: It keeps the formality while marking the season.

tips.text: Use festive reds and greens in muted, deep shades rather than bright ones.
tips.why: Bright seasonal colours quickly look clownish.

tips.text: For an office holiday party, wear your normal work outfit, slightly relaxed and with one seasonal touch.
tips.why: It stays appropriate in front of colleagues while feeling festive.

tips.text: At a conservative office holiday party, pair a dark suit with a pastel shirt rather than plain white.
tips.why: A white shirt can look stuffy at a celebration.

tips.text: With conservative holiday tailoring, wear black cap-toe oxfords or dark brown or oxblood shoes, not light tan.
tips.why: Light tan is too casual for a dark suit.

tips.text: Skip novelty ties with Santa or similar motifs; choose a dark burgundy or muted tie, plain or subtly patterned.
tips.why: Novelty prints look juvenile with tailoring.

tips.text: At a holiday party, the pocket square can be bolder than the tie.
tips.why: It adds festive colour without making the outfit loud.

tips.text: Keep cufflinks, tie bars and rings understated and in matching metals.
In a less formal office, a textured or patterned sport coat (herringbone, houndstooth, tweed or tartan) with flannel or corduroy trousers suits a winter party.
tips.why: Rustic textures feel seasonal while staying smart.

tips.text: For casual offices and house parties, wear a cardigan, cable knit or Fair Isle sweater in warm colours with dark denim or coloured chinos.
tips.why: Cosy knits look festive without needing a suit.

tips.text: Choose an ivory turtleneck over a stark white one.
tips.why: Ivory looks softer and warmer in winter.

tips.text: Bright or playful socks are an easy festive accent at casual holiday gatherings.
tips.why: A small dose of fun that doesn't dominate the outfit.

tips.text: A house party can be more relaxed than the office one, but if the invitation says black tie, wear a dinner suit.
tips.why: The stated dress code always wins.

tips.text: Don't wear a tweed sport coat to a black-tie event.
tips.why: Country tailoring is too casual for evening formal dress.

tips.text: For a festive gala, a burgundy velvet dinner jacket with traditional evening trousers is a seasonal alternative to the black jacket.
tips.why: Velvet and deep colour feel celebratory yet formal.

outfits.outfit: jacket navy smart casual +blazer, sweater cream smart casual, shirt white smart casual, jeans navy casual +dark-wash, boots black smart casual, accessory burgundy +pocket-square
outfits.why: Navy blazer over a cream knit and white shirt with dark denim and black boots suits a holiday house party.

outfits.outfit: sweater brown smart casual +cardigan, shirt cream smart casual +check, tie olive smart formal +knit +silk, trousers brown smart casual +corduroy, dress-shoes brown formal +brogue +derby
outfits.why: Warm browns, a checked cream shirt and an olive knit tie make a relaxed, seasonal look for a casual office or home party.
